analysis.one_liner: Funds nationwide testing for housing discrimination and boosts grants to groups that help victims.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 28-24 along party lines in June 2022, but it never received a vote in the full House before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Department of Housing and Urban Development to run a nationwide testing program that sends matched pairs of renters, homebuyers, and mortgage borrowers to landlords and lenders to detect discrimination based on race, religion, sex, family status, disability, or national origin. It would reauthorize the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, which funds nonprofit groups that assist victims of housing discrimination, at $42.5 million a year through 2025, and add grants to study and test solutions to segregation. After a party-line committee vote in June 2022, the bill never came up for a vote in the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, homebuyers, and mortgage borrowers who face discrimination — including veterans, families with children, women, and people with disabilities — because the government would have documented evidence of discriminatory treatment that can support enforcement actions. Nonprofit fair housing organizations would gain roughly $57.5 million a year in dedicated federal funding to run tests, assist victims, and study segregation.

how_it_helps.text: HUD must run a nationwide program of paired tests to detect and document differences in how renters, homebuyers, and mortgage borrowers are treated based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability status, or national origin [S2] [S3].
The testing results can be used as the basis for federal, state, or local enforcement actions to remedy discriminatory housing practices [S3].

It reauthorizes the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, which supports organizations providing direct assistance to victims of housing discrimination, at $42.5 million per year through fiscal 2025, with at least 75% going to private enforcement work [S2] [S3].

It creates a $5 million-a-year matching grant program for nonprofits to study the causes and effects of housing discrimination and segregation on education, poverty, economic development, and veterans, and to run pilot projects testing solutions [S2] [S3].
HUD would report to Congress every two years on testing outcomes and annually on fair-housing hotline contacts, creating a public record of discrimination patterns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund roughly $62.5 million a year in authorized spending. Landlords, mortgage lenders, and real estate providers bear the cost of being tested and, where discrimination is documented, the risk of enforcement actions. Nonprofit grantees must raise a 50% local match for the study and pilot grants.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes about $62.5 million in new federal spending per year ($15 million for testing, $42.5 million for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, $5 million for grants), all subject to annual appropriations [S3].

Housing providers and lenders face the risk that testers' findings become the basis for investigations and enforcement actions, adding compliance and legal exposure for businesses that may contest the findings [S3].
The study-and-pilot grant program requires a 50% non-federal match, which can exclude smaller nonprofits with limited fundraising capacity [S3].
The funds are restricted from political advocacy and lobbying, and the bill authorizes but does not guarantee funding — Congress must appropriate the money each year for any of it to flow [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest relative to the enforcement capacity it adds: roughly $62.5 million a year to measure and fight discrimination in housing markets worth trillions, much of it flowing through private nonprofits already operating under federal fair housing rules. The main honest objections are that paired testing can produce contested findings that trigger enforcement against housing providers, and that matching-fund requirements tilt grants toward larger organizations. On balance, the bill's costs fall mostly on actors accused of discrimination and on taxpayers at a modest scale, while its benefits accrue to renters and buyers with little independent power to prove unequal treatment.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee voted 28-24 to advance the bill in June 2022, but it was never reported to the House floor or given a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green (D-TX) introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].
On June 22, 2022, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported with amendments by a 28-24 vote [S5].
The bill received no further action and no vote in the full House before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, mortgage lenders, and real estate providers are better off because the bill died: they avoid a permanent federally funded testing program whose findings could support discrimination enforcement. Fair housing nonprofits lost the $57.5 million a year the bill would have authorized for their work.

sides.party_line_note: Every recorded vote and sponsor was Democratic: 28 Democratic cosponsors, and the committee's 28-24 approving vote matched its party split, with Republicans supplying the no votes; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would make these nonprofits the permanent channel for federal fair-housing enforcement money, authorizing $42.5 million a year for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program plus $15 million a year for testing contracts, with at least 75% earmarked for private enforcement work. Their interest in this bill runs directly alongside victims of discrimination [S2] [S3].

Nationwide paired testing could document discriminatory treatment of prospective renters, and those findings can be used as the basis for enforcement actions. Their interest in avoiding documented findings runs against renters' ability to prove discrimination [S3].

The bill extends testing to mortgage lending and refinancing, so lenders' treatment of borrowers of different races, sexes, and other protected classes would be measured and could support enforcement [S3].
Testing covers the home purchase process, so discriminatory practices by real estate professionals could be documented and used in enforcement actions [S3].
